You speak of neighbours, spirit, yet our scouts have seen no smoke but our own. I know of no village called Wewush, and a wise man does not put full trust in a shadow of the night. 

Yet, if these people are truly flesh and blood, and their bellies ache, our granary holds more xi wheat than my people could eat in many harvests. We would gladly share our bounty with strangers in need. But I cannot send a cart into a dream. Which way must my people walk to find their hearths?

I know the wind well enough. It tugs at the hides of our tents and rattles the wood of our huts when the cold months come. 

We have built strong against the wind, and our granaries are heavy with grain. Spirits speak often in the dark, and not all speak true. Why do you trouble my sleep now, when my people are joyful and safe? Speak plainly of what you want, or let me return to my rest.

If you have watched our fields so long, spirit, you would know the seed goes into the earth in spring, not the autumn. My bins burst with wheat, so the harvest does not trouble my mind. I look instead to the cold, for we have many young ones and our tents grow thin. Speak to me of the winter to come, if you truly have sight, or let me wake.

I know the wind that blows in from the sea. It dries our fish on the racks and shakes the hides of our tents, but I have not known it to speak. 

My people are steady, our granaries are heavy with wheat, and we do not chase shadows. If you are a spirit with true knowledge, tell me something useful—perhaps of other villages we might trade with, or new things we might learn to craft. If you have nothing of substance to share, then let me rest. There is real work to be done when the sun rises.

I know of no village called Wewush. My people have walked the coasts and forests, and we have seen no other fires but our own. 

We have much grain, it is true, but it was gathered by the sweat of our own brow to keep our children safe from the lean times. Why do you come in the dark to ask me to feed strangers? If these people are real, speak plain and tell me where they lie, and why I should trust them with the harvest of my village.

I know the wind well enough. It brings the spring rain to our rested fields, and sometimes it tears the hides from our tents, but it does not often speak in words. Why do you come to my sleeping mind tonight, wind-spirit? If you have seen something of worth across the waters or in the deep forests, speak it plainly. Otherwise, you are but empty air passing in the dark.

Where does this Joawethom lie, spirit? And if they are real, what can they offer us in trade for our grain?
